summaries.example: Imagine a science class measures the temperature of water with a thermometer. Another group follows the same steps. If it gets a similar answer, that supports the first result. But if the groups use different thermometers or different water, a different answer may have many possible explanations. Scientists must check what changed before deciding that the first result was wrong.
summaries.summary: Scientific reproducibility is about whether scientific work can be carried out again and whether it gives the same or a suitably similar result. The entry explains that people do not always use words such as replication, repetition, and reproduction in exactly the same way. In computer-based work, reproducibility may mean using the same data and code to get an analysis again. In other fields, it may mean doing an entire experiment again. Repeating work can help scientists check chance results, hidden flaws, fraud, and whether an idea works with different people, tools, or settings. A close repeat tests the earlier result, while a changed repeat can test whether the idea works more generally. If results differ, scientists must ask whether the new study was truly comparable or whether the original claim does not hold. The entry also describes concerns about missing replication studies, selective publishing, unclear methods, and research practices that can make exciting results seem stronger than they are. Open science reforms try to improve this situation through clearer reporting, shared data, public plans, review before results are known, and better rewards for careful work. The larger lesson is that science is strengthened by checking, sharing, and discussing evidence, while remembering that repetition is not a simple yes-or-no test.
key_ideas: Scientists use repeated studies to check whether results were caused by chance, mistakes, or special conditions.
A study can be repeated correctly even when it does not get the same result.
Different kinds of repetition answer different questions, such as whether a result works with new people or new tools.
Some fields have problems because replication studies are rare and reports may leave out important details.
Open science reforms encourage sharing data, registering plans before a study begins, and giving attention to results that do not show a clear effect.
A failed repetition does not automatically prove that the first study was false; scientists must examine how closely the studies matched.
summaries.why_it_matters: People use scientific results to understand the world and make decisions. If results cannot be checked, it is harder to know which claims deserve trust. Careful repetition helps reveal chance findings and mistakes. Sharing methods and data lets more people inspect the work. It also makes science more self-correcting, even though a different result may require thoughtful investigation rather than an instant verdict.

important_terms.definition: Doing a study, experiment, or computer analysis again to see whether its methods and results can be obtained again.
A new attempt to test an earlier scientific study. It may copy the earlier study closely or change some parts.
A mistake or unwanted feature of a study that creates a result that looks real but is caused by something else.
Sharing methods, data, and plans so other people can inspect and try the work.

questions_to_think_about: What would you need to keep the same when repeating a classroom experiment?
If two groups get different answers, what possible changes should they check?
Why might scientists want to share their data and instructions?
Should journals publish studies that find no clear effect? Why?

summaries.example: Suppose a psychology study reports that a brief activity changes test performance. A direct replication uses nearly the same instructions, measures, and kind of participants, mainly testing whether the original finding was reliable. A conceptual replication changes the activity or measure while testing the underlying hypothesis. If the first study succeeds but the second fails, the result might not generalize—or the two studies may not test the same construct. Interpreting the disagreement requires attention to design, measurement, sampling, and background assumptions.
summaries.summary: The entry examines what it means for scientific results to be reproducible and why the concept is difficult to define uniformly. Different disciplines distinguish, or sometimes conflate, rerunning computations, repeating procedures, and obtaining similar results. A study may be reproducible in the weak sense that its methods can be carried out again, without being reproducible in the stronger sense that the same findings result. Typologies of replication therefore vary the site, experimenters, apparatus, operationalizations, or population while pursuing different epistemic goals. Direct replications primarily test the reliability of an earlier empirical result; conceptual replications alter features to examine an underlying hypothesis and its generality. Meta-science has documented concerns in some fields, including scarce replication, publication bias toward significant or novel findings, low statistical power, incomplete reporting, and questionable practices that increase false-positive results. The philosophical discussion asks how replication provides knowledge when experiments always differ. The experimenters’ regress arises because judging a replication may depend on knowing whether its result is correct, while judging the result may depend on knowing whether the replication was properly performed. Responses differ: some stress rational checks and error elimination, while others emphasize tacit knowledge, changing concepts, and social factors. A Bayesian account shows how multiple imperfect replication failures can gradually lower confidence in an original claim without any single failure being decisive. Open science reforms—such as preregistration, data and materials sharing, registered reports, improved peer review, and revised incentives—aim to align scientific
key_ideas: The terms reproduction, repetition, and replication have competing uses across disciplines; computational work may focus on rerunning code, while experimental work may involve new data collection.
Replication has several epistemic functions: checking sampling error, detecting artifacts, examining fraud, testing generalization, and supporting an underlying hypothesis.
Direct and conceptual replication are best understood as points on a continuum, because real studies rarely keep every feature fixed.
Evidence about reproducibility is complicated by publication bias, low statistical power, incomplete reporting, and questionable practices such as p-hacking, cherry-picking, and HARKing.
The experimenters’ regress is a philosophical problem: when results conflict, it may be unclear whether the original claim is wrong or the new study was not a proper replication.

Some philosophers defend rational checks and methodological criticism against this regress; others emphasize the role of tacit knowledge and social conditions in resolving disputes. The entry presents this disagreement without declaring it settled.
summaries.why_it_matters: Reproducibility affects whether evidence can support reliable knowledge, policy, and further research. It also reveals that scientific reliability depends on institutions and incentives, not only on individual honesty. The entry connects technical practices with philosophical questions about evidence, values, and norms. Understanding these links helps readers interpret replication debates without treating one success or failure as a complete verdict.

important_terms.definition: The possibility of carrying out a study or analysis again, often with enough detail about procedures, data, and code to permit checking.
A later investigation related to an earlier one; it may reproduce methods, results, or both, depending on the author’s terminology.
A close repeat intended especially to check whether an earlier result is reliable, including by limiting changes to the original design.
A repeat that changes important features while testing an underlying hypothesis, often to examine generalization or theoretical support.
The extent to which a result is due to the intended experimental manipulation rather than unintended features of the study.
The extent to which a finding applies across different measures, settings, or populations.
The scientific study of science itself, including research methods, reporting, incentives, and reproducibility.
A public, time-stamped record of predictions or methods made before data are collected or analyzed.

questions_to_think_about: Which changes in a replication would test sampling error, and which would test generalization?
When should a failed replication count as evidence against an original claim?
Can a result be reproducible in its methods but not in its findings?
How might publication incentives affect the evidence available to scientists?
Should openness be treated only as a method, or also as a scientific value and norm?

summaries.example: A student team discovers that a certain study routine seems to improve quiz scores. Another team repeats the project with the same instructions, timing, and kind of students. This is a close replication. A third team changes the subject, age group, or way of measuring improvement to see whether the idea works more broadly. If the results differ, students must ask whether the routine failed, whether the groups were different, or whether the projects measured different things.
summaries.summary: Reproducibility asks whether scientific work can be done again and whether it produces the same or a sufficiently similar result. The entry notes that the related words are used differently by different fields and authors. For example, computational researchers may focus on rerunning an analysis with the same data and code, while experimental researchers may repeat the whole study. Repetition can serve several purposes: checking whether a result was due to chance, finding flaws in equipment or design, detecting fraud, seeing whether a finding applies to other groups, and testing the idea behind the original result. A direct replication stays close to the first study. A conceptual replication changes important features to examine whether the underlying idea survives those changes. These categories are not always sharply separated in real research. The entry discusses a reproducibility crisis associated with too few replication studies, selective publication of significant results, low statistical power, incomplete reporting, and questionable research practices. These problems can make false positives—claims of an effect that is not really present—more common. Philosophical questions remain. When two experiments conflict, the new experiment may challenge the original result, or it may not be a proper comparison. The experimenters’ regress describes the difficulty of deciding between those possibilities. Some thinkers emphasize rational tests for errors; others stress tacit skills, changing concepts, and social factors. Reforms linked with open science aim to make research easier to inspect and correct.
key_ideas: Scientists repeat studies for different reasons: to check chance, find flaws, test honesty, or learn whether a finding applies elsewhere.
A study may be repeatable in its procedures but fail to produce the same result.
What counts as reproducibility can differ between fields. In computational work, it may involve rerunning code with shared data; in experimental fields, it may involve redoing a study.
Research can become less trustworthy when journals prefer new positive findings, methods are not fully reported, or researchers use flexible practices to obtain a desired statistical result.
Philosophers disagree about how to interpret conflicting experiments. A disagreement may concern the hypothesis, the quality of the replication, or hidden assumptions about what was measured.
Open science proposals include clearer reports, shared materials and data, preregistration, registered reports, and incentives for careful, transparent work.
summaries.why_it_matters: Scientific findings influence medicine, technology, education, and public decisions, so people need ways to judge how dependable they are. Replication is not a magic test that always settles a question, but it gives researchers more evidence and can expose limits in a claim. Transparent practices also let others learn from results that are mixed or unsuccessful instead of seeing only the most exciting findings.

important_terms.definition: The ability to carry out scientific work again, sometimes meaning that the same methods work and sometimes meaning that similar results appear.
A new study that checks an earlier study or tests its idea under changed conditions.
A replication that stays as close as possible to the earlier study to check its result.
A replication that changes important parts of a study while testing the same basic idea.
A result produced by an unintended feature or flaw rather than by the cause researchers meant to test.
A tendency for studies with exciting or statistically noticeable results to be published more often than studies with unclear results.
A field that studies scientific research in order to evaluate and improve how science is done.
A public record of a study’s predictions or plan made before researchers collect or examine the data.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a journal prefer a new study over a replication?
What is the difference between changing a study to test generality and changing it so much that it tests a different idea?
If a replication fails, what evidence would help you decide what went wrong?
How could preregistration reduce hindsight bias?
Can a scientific system reward researchers for being open and careful while also rewarding exciting discoveries?
